nodes.label: Facts
nodes.question: What are the main sources of energy for residents in the Sichuan Plateau?
nodes.answer: The main sources of energy for residents in the Sichuan Plateau are traditional biomass materials such as firewood, straw, and animal manure.
nodes.paragraph: Different regional climatic conditions lead to great differences in the development of sustainable architecture in different regions 10 15, and the traditional dwellings of ethnic minorities in the Sichuan Plateau have strong regional and historical characteristics, which are valuable non-renewable and irreplaceable historical and cultural heritage in China, and these buildings embody the wisdom of harmonious coexistence between local people and nature, and have extremely high historical and cultural value. However, due to the constraints of climate, topography, and economic development, the local area faces multiple severe challenges such as a lack of conventional energy supply, weak energy infrastructure, and insufficient utilization of renewable energy, including (1) low household energy efficiency. In the Sichuan Plateau, due to the availability of local resources and traditional habits, traditional biomass (firewood, straw, animal manure)16 energy is the main source of energy for residents, and the combustion efficiency of these traditional biomass materials is low, resulting in low energy efficiency. The inefficient combustion process will produce a large amount of smoke and harmful gases, resulting in poor indoor air quality.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Clean energy|Sustainable agriculture energy|Biomass energy for agriculture_qna_003
nodes.label: Strategy
nodes.question: Which type of biochar has had more research focused on its effects on soil fertility and crop yield?
nodes.answer: Far more research has focused on evaluating the benefits of sewage sludge biochar compared to faecal sludge biochar.
nodes.paragraph: This specific type of fertile, very dark, carbon-rich soil, discovered in the Amazon basin, was found to contain greater nutrient content and greater organic carbon content than surrounding soils (Glaser et al., 2001). Biochar as a soil amendment produces many known benefits including improving carbon content and nutrient levels (Glaser et al., 2001), increasing the cation exchange capacity of soils (Glaser et al., 2001), increasing the water-holding capacity of soil (Gaskin et al., 2007; Herath et al., 2013), increasing pH levels in acidic soil (Novak et al., 2009a, 2009b), as well as reducing and immobilizing toxic metals such as arsenic, cadmium and zinc (Park et al., 2011). Biochar application to soil can also provide long-term carbon sequestration, reduce yearly greenhouse emissions and ultimately mitigate climate change (Woolf et al., 2010). Far more research has focused on evaluating the benefits of sewage sludge biochar on soil fertility and crop yield (Gwenzi et al., 2016; Hossain et al., 2015; Khan et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2014a; Sousa & Figueiredo, 2016; Tian et al., 2019; Waqas et al., 2015; You et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2016), compared to faecal sludge biochar (Bai et al., 2018; Woldetsadik et al., 2018).

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Clean energy|Sustainable agriculture energy|Biomass energy for agriculture_qna_004
nodes.label: Taxonomy
nodes.question: What types of agricultural residues are included as raw materials for bioenergy production?
nodes.answer: Agricultural residues include cotton stalks, wheat straw, rice straw, coconut shells, corn stover, and rice husks.
nodes.paragraph: The predomi- nant source of bioenergy is derived from woody wastes, with municipal solid wastes, landfill gases, and agricultural residues also contributing significantly. The agricultural residues include a variety of plant-based materials such as cotton stalks, wheat straw, rice straw, coconut shells, corn stover, and rice husks. These residues represent a substan- tial portion of the raw materials utilized in bioenergy pro- duction [2 , 3]. With the growing emphasis on sustainable energy sources, the thermal conversion of woody biomass has gained prominence. This process not only facilitates the disposal of wood waste but also results in the generation of bioash rich in mineral content, offering potential for nutri- ent recovery and reuse in soil amendment applications. The combustion of woody biomass in fluidized bed systems is a key area of focus in the transition towards more sustainable energy sources. This method of energy generation is par - ticularly appealing due to its ability to efficiently convert a wide range of biomass types into heat and power, while also offering the potential for carbon neutral operations. Gasi- fication encompasses a complex interplay of multi-phase, multi-scale, and multi-physics phenomena, incorporating diverse physical and chemical processes.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Clean energy|Sustainable agriculture energy|Biomass energy for agriculture_qna_005
nodes.label: Facts
nodes.question: Are cover crops and agricultural residues commonly used as exclusive feedstock in biogas plants?
nodes.answer: No, they are not commonly used as exclusive feedstock; the common practice is to co-digest them with animal manure.
nodes.paragraph: 2017). A poten- tial problem with the ensiling of cover crops is their relatively high moisture content at the time of har - vest, which may cause problems for the fermentation. Such problems may be combated by co-ensiling cover crops with straw (Feng et al. 2019). To avoid losses of straw before the harvesting of cover crops and limit the number of field operations, the most viable strat- egy is to harvest the straw at the time of harvest of the main crop and store it until the cover crops also have been harvested (Fontaine et al. 2020a). Cover crops and other agricultural residues are not commonly used as exclusive feedstock in biogas plants (Feng et al. 2020; Thamsiriroj et al. 2012; Xie 215 Nutr Cycl Agroecosyst (2025) 130:213 232 Vol. : (123456789) et al. 2011). Common practice is to co-digest with animal manure (Feng et al. 2020). The implementa- tion of technology for anaerobic digestion of cover crops is thus most feasible at animal farms, where co- digestion with animal manure is possible.
